title: Ὄνος ⟨ἄγριος καὶ ὄνος ἥμερος⟩
titleEn: The Wild Donkey and the Tame Donkey
part: The Wild Donkey and the Tame Donkey (Chambry 264 · Perry 183)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 264 (= Perry 183). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄνος ἄγριος ὄνον ἥμερον θεασάμενος ἔν τινι εὐηλίῳ τόπῳ προσελθὼν ἐμακάριζεν αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τῇ εὐεξίᾳ τοῦ σώματος καὶ τῇ τῆς τροφῆς ἀπολαύσει.
sentences.tr: Onos agrios onon hēmeron theasamenos en tini euēliōi topōi proselthōn emakarizen auton epi tēi euexiāi tou sōmatos kai tēi tēs trophēs apolausei.
sentences.l: A wild donkey, having beheld a tame donkey in a certain sunny place, having approached, was counting him blessed for the good condition of his body and for his enjoyment of his food.
sentences.i: A wild donkey caught sight of a tame one in a sunny spot, came up to him, and called him fortunate for his sleek condition and the good feeding he enjoyed.
sentences.n: Two aorist participles and then an imperfect main verb: the participles supply the steps, the finite verb the thing that goes on. μακαρίζω is to pronounce a man blessed — Greek for envying out loud. εὐεξία is the trained good condition of a body, the word a physician would use.

sentences.t: Ὕστερον δὲ ἰδὼν αὐτὸν ἀχθοφοροῦντα καὶ τὸν ὀνηλάτην ὀπίσω ἑπόμενον καὶ ῥοπάλῳ παίοντα εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε οὐκέτι σε εὐδαιμονίζω· ὁρῶ γὰρ ὅτι οὐκ ἄνευ κακῶν μεγάλων τὴν ἀφθονίαν ἔχεις. »
sentences.tr: Hysteron de idōn auton achthophorounta kai ton onēlatēn opisō hepomenon kai rhopalōi paionta eipen· « All’ egōge ouketi se eudaimonizō· horō gar hoti ouk aneu kakōn megalōn tēn aphthonian echeis. »
sentences.l: But later, having seen him carrying burdens and the donkey-driver following behind and striking him with a club, he said: « Well, I for my part no longer count you happy; for I see that not without great evils do you have your abundance. »
sentences.i: But later he saw him under a load, with the driver at his heels laying on with a club, and said: « Well, I no longer call you fortunate; I see that your plenty does not come to you without great suffering. »
sentences.n: The single aorist ἰδών for the one glance, against present participles (ἀχθοφοροῦντα, ἑπόμενον, παίοντα) for everything that goes on while he looks. οὐκ ἄνευ, 'not without', is Greek understatement, and it is where the fable turns.

sentences.t: Οὕτως οὐκ ἔστι ζηλωτὰ τὰ μετὰ κινδύνων καὶ ταλαιπωριῶν περιγινόμενα κέρδη.
sentences.tr: Houtōs ouk esti zēlōta ta meta kindynōn kai talaipōriōn periginomena kerdē.
sentences.l: So not to be envied are the gains that come in with dangers and hardships.
sentences.n: ζηλωτός is a verbal adjective in -τος, which regularly carries the sense 'to be envied'. περιγίνομαι here is not 'get the better of' but 'come round to one, accrue' — the profit that arrives.
